section.title: Maxima/Minima Problems

learning_objectives.objective: Use partial derivatives to locate critical points for a function of two variables.
Apply a second derivative test to identify a critical point as a local maximum, local minimum, or saddle point for a function of two variables.
Examine critical points and boundary points to find absolute maximum and minimum values for a function of two variables.

section.p: One of the most useful applications for derivatives of a function of one variable is the determination of maximum and/or minimum values. This application is also important for functions of two or more variables, but as we have seen in earlier sections of this chapter, the introduction of more independent variables leads to more possible outcomes for the calculations. The main ideas of finding critical points and using derivative tests are still valid, but new wrinkles appear when assessing the results.

subsection.title: Critical Points
subsection.p: For functions of a single variable, we defined critical points as the values of the function when the derivative equals zero or does not exist. For functions of two or more variables, the concept is essentially the same, except for the fact that we are now working with partial derivatives.

note.p: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a function of two variables that is defined on an open set containing the point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ The point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ is called a critical point of a function of two variables $$f$$ if one of the two following conditions holds:

list.item: Either $$f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\ \text{or}\ f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ does not exist.

subsection.p: The main purpose for determining critical points is to locate relative maxima and minima, as in single-variable calculus. When working with a function of one variable, the definition of a local extremum involves finding an interval around the critical point such that the function value is either greater than or less than all the other function values in that interval. When working with a function of two or more variables, we work with an open disk around the point.

note.p: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a function of two variables that is defined and continuous on an open set containing the point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ Then f has a local maximum at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ if

for all points $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ within some disk centered at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ The number $$f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ is called a local maximum value. If the preceding inequality holds for every point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in the domain of $$f,$$ then $$f$$ has a global maximum (also called an absolute maximum) at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$
The function $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ if

for all points $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ within some disk centered at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ The number $$f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ is called a local minimum value. If the preceding inequality holds for every point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in the domain of $$f,$$ then $$f$$ has a global minimum (also called an absolute minimum) at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$
If $$f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ is either a local maximum or local minimum value, then it is called a local extremum (see the following figure).

subsection.p: In Maxima and Minima, we showed that extrema of functions of one variable occur at critical points. The same is true for functions of more than one variable, as stated in the following theorem.

theorem.title: Fermat’s Theorem for Functions of Two Variables
theorem.p: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a function of two variables that is defined and continuous on an open set containing the point $$(x_{0},y_{0}).$$ Suppose $$f_{x}$$ and $$f_{y}$$ each exists at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ If $$f$$ has a local extremum at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right),$$ then $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ is a critical point of $$f.$$

subsection.title: Second Derivative Test
subsection.p: Consider the function $$f(x) = x^{3}.$$ This function has a critical point at $$x = 0,$$ since $$f\prime(0) = 3(0)^{2} = 0.$$ However, $$f$$ does not have an extreme value at $$x = 0.$$ Therefore, the existence of a critical value at $$x = x_{0}$$ does not guarantee a local extremum at $$x = x_{0}.$$ The same is true for a function of two or more variables. One way this can happen is at a saddle point. An example of a saddle point appears in the following figure.

image.alt: The function z = x2 – y2 is shown, which is roughly saddle looking, with the function achieving maxima along the x and y axes.
image.caption: Graph of the function $$z = x^{2} - y^{2}.$$ This graph has a saddle point at the origin.

subsection.p: In this graph, the origin is a saddle point. This is because the first partial derivatives of $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} - y^{2}$$ are both equal to zero at this point, but it is neither a maximum nor a minimum for the function. Furthermore the vertical trace corresponding to $$y = 0$$ is $$z = x^{2}$$ (a parabola opening upward), but the vertical trace corresponding to $$x = 0$$ is $$z = \text{−}y^{2}$$ (a parabola opening downward). Therefore, it is both a global maximum for one trace and a global minimum for another.

note.p: Given the function $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right),$$ the point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0},f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} \right)$$ is a saddle point if both $$f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = 0$$ and $$f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = 0,$$ but $$f$$ does not have a local extremum at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$

subsection.p: The second derivative test for a function of one variable provides a method for determining whether an extremum occurs at a critical point of a function. When extending this result to a function of two variables, an issue arises related to the fact that there are, in fact, four different second-order partial derivatives, although equality of mixed partials reduces this to three. The second derivative test for a function of two variables, stated in the following theorem, uses a discriminant $$D$$ that replaces $$f^{''}\left( x_{0} \right)$$ in the second derivative test for a function of one variable.

theorem.title: Second Derivative Test
theorem.p: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a function of two variables for which the first- and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on some disk containing the point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ Suppose $$f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = 0$$ and $$f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = 0.$$ Define the quantity

list.item: If $$D > 0$$ and $$f_{xx}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) > 0,$$ then $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$
If $$D > 0$$ and $$f_{xx}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) < 0,$$ then $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$
If $$D < 0,$$ then $$f$$ has a saddle point at $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$
If $$D = 0,$$ then the test is inconclusive.

image.alt: This figure consists of three figures labeled a, b, and c. Figure a has two bulbous mounds pointing down, and the two extrema are listed as the local minima. Figure b has two bulbous mounds pointed up, and the two extrema are listed as the local maxima. Figure c is shaped like a saddle, and in the middle of the saddle, a point is marked as the saddle point.
image.caption: The second derivative test can often determine whether a function of two variables has a local minima (a), a local maxima (b), or a saddle point (c).

subsection.p: To apply the second derivative test, it is necessary that we first find the critical points of the function. There are several steps involved in the entire procedure, which are outlined in a problem-solving strategy.

note.p: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a function of two variables for which the first- and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on some disk containing the point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ To apply the second derivative test to find local extrema, use the following steps:

list.item: Determine the critical points $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ of the function $$f$$ where $$f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = 0.$$ Discard any points where at least one of the partial derivatives does not exist.
Calculate the discriminant $$D = f_{xx}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)f_{yy}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) - \left( {f_{xy}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} \right)^{2}$$ for each critical point of $$f.$$
Apply Second Derivative Test to determine whether each critical point is a local maximum, local minimum, or saddle point, or whether the theorem is inconclusive.

subsection.title: Absolute Maxima and Minima
subsection.p: When finding global extrema of functions of one variable on a closed interval, we start by checking the critical values over that interval and then evaluate the function at the endpoints of the interval. When working with a function of two variables, the closed interval is replaced by a closed, bounded set. A set is bounded if all the points in that set can be contained within a ball (or disk) of finite radius. First, we need to find the critical points inside the set and calculate the corresponding critical values. Then, it is necessary to find the maximum and minimum value of the function on the boundary of the set. When we have all these values, the largest function value corresponds to the global maximum and the smallest function value corresponds to the absolute minimum. First, however, we need to be assured that such values exist. The following theorem does this.

theorem.title: Extreme Value Theorem
theorem.p: A continuous function $$f(x,y)$$ on a closed and bounded set $$D$$ in the plane attains an absolute maximum value at some point of $$D$$ and an absolute minimum value at some point of $$D.$$

subsection.p: Now that we know any continuous function $$f$$ defined on a closed, bounded set attains its extreme values, we need to know how to find them.

theorem.title: Finding Extreme Values of a Function of Two Variables
theorem.p: Assume $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a differentiable function of two variables defined on a closed, bounded set $$D.$$ Then $$f$$ will attain the absolute maximum value and the absolute minimum value, which are, respectively, the largest and smallest values found among the following:

list.item: The values of $$f$$ at the critical points of $$f$$ in $$D.$$
The values of $$f$$ on the boundary of $$D.$$

subsection.p: The proof of this theorem is a direct consequence of the extreme value theorem and Fermat’s theorem. In particular, if either extremum is not located on the boundary of $$D,$$ then it is located at an interior point of $$D.$$ But an interior point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ of $$D$$ that’s an absolute extremum is also a local extremum; hence, $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ is a critical point of $$f$$ by Fermat’s theorem. Therefore the only possible values for the global extrema of $$f$$ on $$D$$ are the extreme values of $$f$$ on the interior or boundary of $$D.$$

note.p: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a continuous function of two variables defined on a closed, bounded set $$D,$$ and assume $$f$$ is differentiable on $$D.$$ To find the absolute maximum and minimum values of $$f$$ on $$D,$$ do the following:

list.item: Determine the critical points of $$f$$ in $$D.$$
Calculate $$f$$ at each of these critical points.
Determine the maximum and minimum values of $$f$$ on the boundary of its domain.
The maximum and minimum values of $$f$$ will occur at one of the values obtained in steps $$2\ \text{and}\ 3.$$

subsection.p: Finding the maximum and minimum values of $$f$$ on the boundary of $$D$$ can be challenging. If the boundary is a rectangle or set of straight lines, then it is possible to parameterize the line segments and determine the maxima on each of these segments, as seen in Example 4.40. The same approach can be used for other shapes such as circles and ellipses.

If the boundary of the set $$D$$ is a more complicated curve defined by a function $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = c$$ for some constant $$c,$$ and the first-order partial derivatives of $$g$$ exist, then the method of Lagrange multipliers can prove useful for determining the extrema of $$f$$ on the boundary. The method of Lagrange multipliers is introduced in Lagrange Multipliers.

problem.p: Pro-$$z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = 48x + 96y - x^{2} - 2xy - 9y^{2},$$ company has developed a profit model that depends on the number x of golf balls sold per month (measured in thousands), and the number of hours per month of advertising y, according to the function

where $$50,000,$$ is measured in thousands of dollars. The maximum number of golf balls that can be produced and sold is $$25.$$ and the maximum number of hours of advertising that can be purchased is $$x$$ Find the values of $$y$$ and $$1$$ that maximize profit, and find the maximum profit.

solution.p: Using the problem-solving strategy, step $$f$$ involves finding the critical points of $$f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ on its domain. Therefore, we first calculate $$f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right),$$ and $$\begin{array}{rll} {f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {48 - 2x - 2y} \\ {f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {96 - 2x - 18y.} \end{array}$$ then set them each equal to zero:
Setting them equal to zero yields the system of equations

The solution to this system is $$y = 3.$$ and $$\left( {21,3} \right)$$ Therefore $$f.$$ is a critical point of $$f\left( {21,3} \right)$$ Calculating $$f\left( {21,3} \right) = 48(21) + 96(3) - 21^{2} - 2(21)(3) - 9(3)^{2} = 648.$$ gives $$0 \leq x \leq 50$$
The domain of this function is $$0 \leq y \leq 25$$ and $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 48x + 96y - x^{2} - 2xy - 9y^{2}.$$ as shown in the following graph.

image.alt: A rectangle is drawn in the first quadrant with one corner at the origin, horizontal length 50, and height 25. This rectangle is marked D, and the sides are marked in counterclockwise order from the side overlapping the x axis L1, L2, L3, and L4.

solution.p: $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is the line segment connecting $$\left( {50,0} \right),$$ and $$x(t) = t,y(t) = 0$$ and it can be parameterized by the equations $$0 \leq t \leq 50.$$ for $$g(t) = f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)\text{:}$$ We then define $$\begin{array}{cl} {g(t)} & {= f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {t,0} \right)} \\ & {= 48t + 96(0) - t^{2} - 2(t)(0) - 9(0)^{2}} \\ & {= 48t - t^{2}.} \end{array}$$
Setting $$t = 24,$$ yields the critical point $$\left( {24,0} \right)$$ which corresponds to the point $$f.$$ in the domain of $$f\left( {24,0} \right)$$ Calculating $$576.$$ gives $$L_{2}$$

$$\left( {50,25} \right),$$ is the line segment connecting $$x(t) = 50,y(t) = t$$ and $$0 \leq t \leq 25.$$ and it can be parameterized by the equations $$g(t) = f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)\text{:}$$ for $$\begin{array}{cl} {g(t)} & {= f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {50,t} \right)} \\ & {= 48(50) + 96t - 50^{2} - 2(50)t - 9t^{2}} \\ & {= -9t^{2} - 4t - 100.} \end{array}$$ Once again, we define $$t = - \frac{2}{9},$$
This function has a critical point at $$f.$$ which corresponds to the point $$L_{3}$$ This point is not in the domain of $$\left( {0,25} \right)\ \text{and}\ \left( {50,25} \right),$$

$$x(t) = t,y(t) = 25$$ is the line segment connecting $$0 \leq t \leq 50.$$ and it can be parameterized by the equations $$g(t) = f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)\text{:}$$ for $$\begin{array}{cl} {g(t)} & {= f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {t,25} \right)} \\ & {= 48t + 96(25) - t^{2} - 2t(25) - 9\left( 25^{2} \right)} \\ & {= \text{−}t^{2} - 2t - 3225.} \end{array}$$ We define $$t = -1,$$
This function has a critical point at $$L_{4}$$ which corresponds to the point $$\left( {0,0} \right)\ \text{to}\ \left( {0,25} \right),$$ which is not in the domain.

$$x(t) = 0,y(t) = t$$ is the line segment connecting $$0 \leq t \leq 25.$$ and it can be parameterized by the equations $$g(t) = f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)\text{:}$$ for $$\begin{array}{cl} {g(t)} & {= f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {0,t} \right)} \\ & {= 48(0) + 96t - (0)^{2} - 2(0)t - 9t^{2}} \\ & {= 96t - t^{2}.} \end{array}$$ We define $$t = \frac{16}{3},$$

This function has a critical point at $$f\left( {0,\frac{16}{3}} \right)$$ which corresponds to the point $$256.$$ which is on the boundary of the domain. Calculating $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ gives $$\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {50,0} \right),\left( {50,25} \right)\ \text{and}\ \left( {0,25} \right)\text{:}$$

The maximum critical value is $$\text{\$}648,000$$ which occurs at $$21,000$$ Therefore, a maximum profit of $$3$$ is realized when $$f(x,y)$$ golf balls are sold and $$\left( {21,3,648} \right).$$ hours of advertising are purchased per month as shown in the following figure.
